articles.title: Mary Jane Veloso on her freedom, family reunion: 'Ito 'yung araw na pinakahihintay ko'
articles.summary: Mary Jane Veloso on her freedom, family reunion: 'Ito 'yung araw na pinakahihintay ko"

blocks.text: Former overseas Filipino worker (OFW) Mary Jane Veloso expressed her joy after she was granted absolute pardon, released from prison and reunited with her family.
In a press conference, Veloso was asked how she felt upon seeing her kin following her release.
“Namamaga na po ang mata ko. Kasi sa sobrang saya, kasama iyak. Kasi sabi ko nga po na ito ‘yung araw na pinakahihintay ko. At dumating na po siya, ibinigay na po sa akin ni God," Veloso said.
(My eyes are already swollen. Because I was so happy, I also cried. Because I said this was the day I had been waiting for. And it has arrived, God has given it to me.)
"Kaya sobrang masayang-masaya. Hindi po siya maipapaliwanag lang ng salita. Pero sa kilos naman po siguro namin, alam po ninyo na sobrang halaga ng araw po na ito sa amin lahat,” she added.
(That's why I'm so happy. Words can't explain it. Perhaps through our actions, you know that this day is very important for all of us.)

Veloso had an emotional reunion with her family early Saturday. Mary Jane's family members were fetched from Nueva Ecija and brought to the Correctional Institution for Women (CIW) in Mandaluyong City to meet her.
Following their reunion, Mary Jane said she currently has no plans but to rest and be with her family.
“Pahinga po muna. ‘Yun po kasi una talagang gagawin, pahinga po muna. Pero po pahihintulutan po ng Panginoong Diyos, baka po bukas magsimba kami,”
(I’ll rest first. That's what I'll do first, to rest first. But God willing, maybe we'll go to Church tomorrow.)

Asked what they will eat as a family once they return home, Mary Jane answered, “Pinakbet! Inihaw na isda tsaka pinakbet po. Para healthy naman ‘yung pagkain ko. Kasi po mahilig ako mag-noodles noong nasa CIW ako.”
(Pinakbet! Grilled fish and pinakbet. So that my food will be healthy. Because I was taking noodles when I was in CIW.)
“Pero ‘yung Pinakbet kasi nina nanay, nina ate, magagaling po sila magluto ‘yung pamilya ko. Ako lang po ‘di marunong magluto. Masarap po ‘yung kanilang pinakbet,” she added.
(My mother's and my sister's Pinakbet is good, my family is good with cooking. I'm the only one who doesn't know how to cook. Their Pinakbet is delicious.)
CIW
Asked about her unforgettable memory during her stay at the CIW, Mary Jane said: “Pag-aaral (Studies).

“Kasi po nu’ng nasa Indonesia ko, hindi ko po natutukan ‘yung pag-aaral doon… Hindi po siya katulad ng sa Pilipinas na talagang ang prioridad po nila ay edukasyon. Sa Indonesia po kasi ang prioridad nila talaga ay livelihood,” she said.
(Because when I was in Indonesia, I was not able to focus on my studies ... It's not like in the Philippines where education is a priority. In Indonesia, their priority is livelihood.)
During her timeint prison, Mary Jane said she was granted Good Conduct Time Allowance (GCTA) and underwent TASTM (Time Allowance for Study, Teaching, and Mentoring).

“Napilitan po ako talaga noong una. Sinabi ko din po na napilitan ako. Pero parang ayoko talaga. Pero maniwala man po kayo sa hindi, na-enjoy ko ‘yung pag-aaral ko… Sa English lang talaga ako medyo mahina. Pero sa Math, sa Science, enjoy po ako.”

(I was hesitant to go at first. I also said that I was forced. It's like I really didn't want to. But believe it or not, I enjoyed my studies… I'm not so good with English. But in Math, in Science, I enjoyed it.)

Mary Jane was arrested on April 25, 2010, at Adisutjipto International Airport in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, after authorities found 2.6 kilograms of heroin in her luggage. She was sentenced to death by an Indonesian court on October 11, 2010.
She has consistently maintained her innocence, saying she was unknowingly used as a drug courier after being given a suitcase by her recruiters.
Her execution was halted in April 2015 after the Philippine government appealed to Indonesian authorities to allow her to testify against her alleged recruiters.

In December 2024, Indonesia agreed to transfer Mary Jane to Philippine custody following years of diplomatic negotiations. She arrived in the Philippines on December 18, 2024, and was transferred to CIW to serve the remainder of her sentence under Philippine jurisdiction.
Mary Jane was formally released from CIW on Friday after the necessary procedures were completed. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Whistleblower alleges millions of Driscoll’s berries sent to Canada with excess chemical levels
articles.summary: A whistleblower lawsuit in California is alleging millions of pounds of Driscoll's fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border into Canada, and the company…

image.caption: A pack of Driscoll’s raspberries sold in Montreal. A whistleblower lawsuit is alleging millions of pounds of the company's fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border into Canada, and the company tried to cover it up. (Gloria Henríquez/CBC News)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

A whistleblower lawsuit in California is alleging millions of pounds of Driscoll's fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border into Canada, and the company tried to cover it up.
Lawsuit claims about 50% of shipments from 2022-24 had fruit exceeding Canadian safety levels
Driscoll’s berries are on many Canadians’ plates and all over Canadian grocery stores, with their tagline claiming to be “only the finest berries.”

But a whistleblower lawsuit in California alleges the finest berries were not sent to Canada: instead, millions of pounds of fruit containing non-compliant levels of pesticides and chemicals crossed the border, and the company tried to cover it up.

California resident and former Driscoll’s employee David Harada claims in the lawsuit that by Driscoll’s own estimates, about 50 per cent of all shipments to Canada from 2022 to 2024 had fruit that exceeded Canadian safety levels.
“And it's something where you start seeing it so regularly and you know that something's not right that you have to speak up,” Harada said in an interview with CBC News.

Harada was Driscoll’s manager of food safety and regulatory compliance for the U.S. and Canada. He filed a lawsuit for unlawful retaliation against Driscoll’s. In the lawsuit’s filing, Harada said he felt that he was being set up to be the “scapegoat” for compliance issues and that he was being retaliated against for speaking up.

Harada told CBC he first started noticing problems regarding pesticide safety and over-application in 2022 and reported them immediately to his bosses. He says he brought his concerns to upper management but was told it was something he’d have to manage.
“I had a conversation with my director as to whether or not they had plausible deniability regarding this issue,” Harada said.
CFIA inspected Driscoll’s berries sold across Canada

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) confirmed to CBC News it conducted several inspections on Driscoll’s berries sold in grocery stores across the country between 2022-24 and found chemical levels above the legal limit in Canada.
The chemicals include bifenthrin, iprodione and captan: fungicides and insecticides.
However, the CFIA says the inspections did not lead to recalls, or a corrective action was implemented and the investigations were closed.

items: Independent scientist resigns from pesticide regulator over transparency concerns

blocks.text: Some investigations were also triggered after reports of suspected illness after eating Driscoll's blueberries, or by complaints of chemical taste and smell. The CFIA said the reported illness could not be definitively linked to the berries.

“The cases you have identified involve different products, pesticide residues, importers and locations over a period of several years,” the CFIA wrote in an email to CBC News. “The presence of the Driscoll’s brand on the products does not, on its own, establish that the non-compliances originated from a single producer or source.”
The CFIA says it takes appropriate action depending on the magnitude of the health risk.
Whistleblower alleges Driscoll’s sent millions of berries with excess chemical levels to Canada
Actions include notifying the producer or importer, the specific supplier and follow-up inspections.
Recalls are issued if Health Canada determines that a product poses an unacceptable health risk.
What are the health risks from tainted berries?
Stéphane Bayen, an associate professor in the department of food science and agricultural chemistry at McGill University says berries are often found to have chemical residues above the legal limit.
“That's not something abnormal completely, but definitely that's not what we would like to see and we want to reduce this,” Bayen said.

“Exceedance one time of the maximum residue limit might not be translated as a risk for the health of consumers. That’s where the discussion needs to happen and to make sure that this is not becoming a regular thing.”
Toxicologist Daniel Green says the levels of chemicals found in the CFIA-tested berries wouldn’t make someone sick from eating just a few.
“To get an effect, one would have to eat 19 kilograms,” Green said from one example.
Green says the problem is the exposure to all other toxins combined over time: from food and the environment.
“It is the chemical lifetime exposure experience that has to be looked at,” Green said.

items: Fresh strawberries were a summer luxury. When did they become an all-season toddler snack?
Carney government passes law allowing authorization of banned pesticides

blocks.text: That’s what worries Harada and motivated him to speak out.
He believes the potentially tainted berries crossed the border because in 2022, Driscoll’s removed the food safety and compliance tracking system it had for Canada in order to sell more here.

Harada says that the system ensures there is enough time between the last application of pesticides on the fruit and when it's picked — which allows enough time for chemicals to break down, preventing residues from being over the legal limit.

He accused Driscoll's of wilfully concealing information about the berries’ toxicity levels and told them in order to fix all the issues, the company needed to go public about the violations and potential harms and issue recalls.
“I completely believe that I was part of a coverup because they chose not to disclose this information publicly,” Harada told CBC News.
Driscoll’s says it ‘responded correctly’
Even though Harada says the company asked him to reinstate the tracking system, they didn’t go public and he says he was pushed to resign.

In an email to CBC, Driscoll’s says it cannot comment on the details of Harada’s employment due to confidentiality issues. But it said it “remains confident that the complete factual record will demonstrate that it responded correctly to the concerns Mr. Harada raised, at all times acted in good faith, and at all times conducted itself appropriately."
It also denies removing the food safety tracking system and other allegations in Harada’s lawsuit, adding the company has never knowingly shipped products it believed to be unsafe.

“There will be an appropriate time in the litigation for Driscoll’s to present its own evidence, which we believe will show a very different picture from the one Mr. Harada has presented publicly,” Driscoll’s statement read in part.
Harada says it has not been easy living with the stigma of being a whistleblower, but he thinks it was the right call.
“Canada as a whole deserves more and consumers of any products deserve to feel safe when consuming it,” he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Gloria has been a journalist in Montreal for more than a decade. Prior to joining CBC, she reported in three languages and five different countries for Global News, France 24, Berliner Zeitung and Diario La Tribuna in her native Honduras.

articles.title: What Canada's wastewater reveals about drug use in 8 cities
articles.summary: New StatCan data shows sharply different drug-use patterns across eight Canadian cities, with methamphetamine elevated in parts of the Prairies and Moncton, cocaine comparatively high in Halifax and…

image.caption: A woman smokes drugs from a pipe on Dundas Street in downtown London, Ont., in August 2026. The latest StatCan figures offer a window into which drugs are showing up most prominently in different communities. (Alessio Donnini/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

New StatCan data shows sharply different drug-use patterns across eight Canadian cities, with methamphetamine elevated in parts of the Prairies and Moncton, cocaine comparatively high in Halifax and fentanyl highest in Metro Vancouver.
New StatCan data shows starkly different drug-use patterns across 8 Canadian cities
Flush a toilet in Prince Albert, Sask., and the wastewater tells a very different drug story than it does in Halifax or Vancouver.
New Statistics Canada data shows striking differences in drugs detected in wastewater across eight Canadian cities:

items: Methamphetamine and cocaine levels were highest in Prince Albert and also elevated in Saskatoon and Moncton, N.B.
Halifax had the lowest methamphetamine levels but comparatively high cocaine levels.
Fentanyl remained dramatically higher in Metro Vancouver than elsewhere.

blocks.text: The StatCan survey measures drug metabolites — chemical byproducts excreted after the body breaks down drugs — in wastewater samples collected during one-week sampling windows every two months.
The data, from January 2024 to March 2026, covers catchments serving about 9.2 million people. StatCan cautions that it doesn't show exactly how many people use a drug or how much they consume.
But it is a "pretty good proxy of drug consumption" within the area served by a treatment plant, StatCan analyst Sianne Kuang told CBC News.
Prince Albert
Prince Albert had the highest methamphetamine levels of any city monitored and the greatest fluctuations in both methamphetamine and cocaine.
In March 2026, its estimated methamphetamine load was 2,003 milligrams per 1,000 people per day — more than nine times Toronto's roughly 214 milligrams.

"There's many different drivers of different substance use, and one of them is just what is available in the market," said Kora DeBeck, a professor in the School of Public Policy at Simon Fraser University.
Saskatoon
Saskatoon also recorded some of the highest methamphetamine levels, along with Moncton, but behind Prince Albert. Its March 2026 reading was about 958 milligrams per 1,000 people per day.
DeBeck said regional patterns may be connected to how drugs reach local markets.
"It seems much more connected to drug trafficking and how the networks of drug production and trafficking work, and we really don't have good insight into that."
Edmonton
Edmonton's methamphetamine load reached about 1,071 milligrams per 1,000 people per day in January 2025 and stood at 624 in March 2026 — nearly three times Toronto's level that month.
Moncton
Moncton also recorded some of the highest methamphetamine levels.
Methamphetamine was involved in 63 per cent of stimulant toxicity deaths in New Brunswick in 2024 — the highest share involving methamphetamine among Atlantic provinces, StatCan noted.
Moncton joined the survey in March 2025, providing less data from which to identify trends.
Halifax

In March 2026, it recorded just 56 milligrams of methamphetamine per 1,000 people per day, the lowest among the cities monitored, while cocaine was about 1,734 milligrams. Prince Albert's cocaine reading was about 5,296 milligrams — roughly three times Halifax's.

Cocaine was involved in 86 per cent of stimulant-related deaths in Nova Scotia in 2024, compared with 14 per cent involving methamphetamine. Earlier CBC reporting also documented cocaine's growing role in drug-related deaths in the province.
Monty Ghosh, an addiction physician and researcher at the University of Alberta, said local production, using different precursors, formulas and mixtures, can create distinct regional supplies.
"They don't have the same formula they're using. They don't use necessarily the same compounds or drugs."
Metro Vancouver
Metro Vancouver consistently recorded the highest fentanyl levels of all eight cities.
Average levels declined in 2025 and early 2026 compared with 2024, a change StatCan says coincided with a drop in Vancouver's unregulated drug death rate.
DeBeck cautioned against viewing fentanyl's prevalence simply as a response to demand.
"People didn't demand or want fentanyl in the beginning. It just arrived and was there, and then people became dependent on it," she said.

Ghosh said falling fentanyl measurements don't necessarily capture everything happening in the opioid supply, noting that "there's different forms of fentanyl out there, which may not be measured here."
Toronto
Toronto's methamphetamine levels were far below those recorded in Prince Albert and Saskatoon, but another stimulant stood out.
Across available reporting months from July 2024 to March 2026, Toronto had the highest average MDMA levels of the eight cities, at about 40 milligrams per 1,000 people per day.
Montreal
Montreal stood out for comparatively low levels of several opioids measured in the study.
Its codeine levels were the lowest among the participating cities, never exceeding about 44 milligrams per 1,000 people per day, compared with a combined-city average ranging from about 97 to 219.
Montreal also recorded the lowest methadone levels and some of the lowest oxycodone and morphine readings.
Its stimulant profile was closer to Toronto's, with relatively low methamphetamine and comparatively higher MDMA readings.
Wastewater can help illuminate patterns, Ghosh said, but it shouldn't be read in isolation.
"It's only one part of the picture."
Commuting, tourism and temporary population changes caused by special events can introduce uncertainty into the estimates, StatCan cautions.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eric Michael Johnson is a senior writer and editor based in Vancouver. Before joining CBC, he was an award-winning science writer and editor. He holds a PhD in the history of science from the University of British Columbia. He can be reached at eric.johnson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Why is it so difficult for Ukraine to take down Russia's jet-powered drones?
articles.summary: Russia's jet-powered drones being used to carry out strikes on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine are often able to evade air defences because they fly at higher altitudes and faster speeds. To stop…

image.caption: Firefighters work around the debris of what appears to be a jet-powered drone engine following a Russian strike on Kyiv Friday. (Angela Johnston/CBC)

blocks.text: World·New

Russia's jet-powered drones being used to carry out strikes on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine are often able to evade air defences because they fly at higher altitudes and faster speeds. To stop these new models, faster interceptors are needed, but that technology is still in the trial phase, Ukrainian officials say.
Half of drones currently being launched at Ukraine are jet-powered, senior official suggests

When a Russian drone slammed into a high-rise residential building in Kyiv around 8 a.m. Friday, killing a 14-year-old boy and injuring several others, the remnants of a jet engine were plainly visible among the broken glass and blackened debris on the pavement.
Russia's latest battlefield innovation — jet-powered drones — has been used to carry out strikes on the Ukrainian capital, including attacks targeting offices, data centres and warehouses.

The weapons, which have been pummelling Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine for weeks, have often been able to evade Ukrainian air defences because they fly at higher altitudes and at much higher speeds, reaching more than 600 km/h.
"It's not easy to intercept. You need to intercept [at] a similar speed or faster," said Volodymyr Khomenko, head of the Explosive Ordnance Disposal Department of the National Police of Ukraine.
"For faster drones, we need faster interceptors."
24 hours in Kyiv: Living through Russian drone strikes
What are jet-powered drones?
According to Ukrainian officials, Russia began testing its jet-powered strike drones two years ago in the Chernihiv region, north of Kyiv and near the border with Belarus.

Unlike earlier models of Shahed drones, which were based on Iranian designs and included piston engines, the new versions are equipped with turbojet engines. Ukrainian military intelligence officials have said some of those engines are being sourced from China.

There are three models of Geran jet-powered drones, with the latest being the Geran-5. Its design differs significantly from earlier versions. Instead of a triangular shape, it looks more like a cruise missile, with aerodynamic fins.
The Geran-5 can cruise at about 600 km/h, roughly three times the speed of the earlier Shahed models that began attacking Ukrainian cities in 2022.
How often is Russia using them?

Khomenko told CBC News that he believes about half of the drones currently being launched at Ukraine are jet-powered, while the other half are older models. But he says the balance is shifting rapidly.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia fired 2,800 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in August, almost twice as many as in July.

In recent weeks, Russia has been sending the drones in small waves, often resulting in multihour air-raid alerts in Kyiv. Air defences can be heard throughout the city alongside the sound of explosions.

Unlike older models, which emit a buzzing sound that's been compared to a motorcycle, the jet-powered drones are quieter. Instead, residents often report hearing a whooshing sound as they fly through the air.

items: Ukraine's largest steel plant to shutter amid recurring Russian strikes
Russian drones are stalking Ukrainian trains and trying to hobble the country's rail system

blocks.text: When a drone crashed into the high-rise apartment building on Friday, Alice Boyko told CBC News she didn't think she heard the air-raid siren until after the explosion. She lives in the same building that was struck, but her apartment is on the opposite side.
"To be honest, I was more afraid of the missiles, but now I worry about drones, too.
"You never think that this is going to happen to you."
Why are they so hard for air defences to intercept?
Ukraine's Air Force has said that it's intercepting about 60 per cent of the jet-powered drones, compared with more than 90 per cent of earlier models.

During air-raid alerts in Kyiv, mobile units armed with heavy machine guns and shoulder-mounted surface-to-air missile systems track threats in the sky. Above them, fighter jets, including F-16s, try to shoot the drones down.
Ukraine has also developed a large fleet of interceptor drones during the war. But the models currently in the field are not fast enough to intercept the jet-powered drones.

Borys Dolyna, a commander of a Ukrainian interceptor-drone company, told CBC News that the jet-powered drones move so quickly that they can be difficult to see even on the video feeds from interceptor drones. In some cases, he says, they appear as little more than a small pixel on the screen.
He says he's seen jet-powered drones several times, but their speed was so great that his team had no chance of intercepting them.
What is Ukraine doing about it?
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the country is trying to accelerate production of newly designed interceptors capable of bringing down the Russian drones.
While officials have reported a number of successful interceptions, the technology is still in the trial phase.

Cory Woods, a Canadian working as a drone-interceptor pilot in Ukraine who is normally deployed in the eastern part of the country closer to the front, says drone warfare is evolving so rapidly that it has become what he describes as a "cat-and-mouse game."
"Every time the enemy makes an innovation and alters their technology or their tactics, we have to respond and change ours," he said in an interview with CBC News from Kyiv.
"Once they pick up on that, they change it again, and so it's constantly going back and forth."

However, Woods says that if Ukraine is to seriously blunt Russia's ability to use strike drones across the country, its military must have weapons capable of targeting the factories where the drones are made and the sites where they're launched.

items: Ukraine fires more than 1,000 drones at Russia, including hundreds launched at Moscow
The moment a Russian drone bypassed Ukrainian air defences

blocks.text: "There's no point in hitting the arrow if you let the archer live," he said.
"Russia has massive manufacturing capabilities. They've been gearing up for this for years. They've stockpiled a lot."
One of Russia's deadly jet-powered drones crashed in this backyard
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Briar Stewart is a CBC correspondent, based in London. During her nearly two decades with CBC, she has reported across Canada and internationally. She can be reached at briar.stewart@cbc.ca or on X @briarstewart.

articles.title: What is the truth about Diana? Her brother offers his view, ‘once and for all’
articles.summary: The recent publication of a book by Charles Spencer, the younger brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, has only added to the way in which her legacy will keep being a focus of debate and…

image.caption: Copies of Charles Spencer's book Swan Song: Diana, my sister are displayed at a bookshop in central London on Tuesday. (Jack Taylor/Reuters)

blocks.text: In the opening pages of his tribute to his sister, Charles Spencer makes a simple vow.
The younger brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, promises that he will "tell things how I remember them, lay them down for good, once and for all."

The book is entitled Swan Song: Diana, my sister. In those words, there is a pledge that these recollections will be his last sharing of what he recalls of his big sister, a high-wattage celebrity royal whose personal struggles and open way made an emotional connection with many who watched her from afar.

Time will tell if that is indeed the case. But there is little doubt that the book — published Tuesday amid a mad swirl of headlines around its claims — has only added to the way in which Diana's legacy will keep being a focus of debate and interpretation nearly 30 years after her sudden and shocking death in 1997.

Beyond those claims — perhaps the most incendiary being that King Charles said his former wife would soon be forgotten after her death — the book does offer new anecdotes and insights into Diana, particularly in the early years she shared with her little brother.

But more broadly, the book raises additional questions over recent history within the upper echelons of the Royal Family, and ultimately reflects the impossibility of ever fully knowing exactly what Diana thought or felt.

Much media attention has focused on select claims in the book, including that Diana told her brother that Charles said he wasn't in love with her before their wedding and that Queen Elizabeth offered to restore her HRH title shortly after her death. Spencer also writes that he believed that the royals weren't properly supporting Charles and Diana's younger son, Prince Harry, in the days immediately following her death.
A rare royal response

The usual royal position of not commenting in times like this means we are unlikely to ever hear an official response to much of what Spencer says in connection with actions of senior members of the Royal Family.
But the first published excerpt of the book, which included the assertion that Charles said Diana would soon be forgotten, did provoke an unusually quick comment.

items: Buckingham Palace hits back at claims in a book by Princess Diana’s brother

blocks.text: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," the statement from Buckingham Palace said.
King Charles addresses claims he was dismissive about Princess Diana's death

That response set off a debate of its own and launched comparisons with Queen Elizabeth's "recollections may vary" response to claims made by Harry and his wife Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, in their interview with Oprah Winfrey.
What was she actually like?

All this leaves those watching from afar to come to their own conclusions, caught amid contradictions and varying views. And it all drifts away from the more fundamental question those with an interest in Diana herself may have and may have hoped to find answers for within Spencer's book: What was she actually like?

items: Diana's legacy: Why it still resonates 25 years after her death

blocks.text: In Spencer's accounting of their younger years together, those looking for details will be rewarded. Some are simple and speak to happy, ordinary moments in a young life — Diana liked to keep her room in perfect order, she tended to her stuffed toys with devotion, she loved flowers.

Others are darker or more complicated, whether it's Spencer's recollections of abuse at the hand of a nanny or a rare moment of youthful discord between the siblings, when Diana shoved her brother off his bike.
Diana's brother doubles down on scathing King Charles allegations

Such level of detail lessens as Spencer's account progresses, perhaps rooted in the fact that his proximity to his sister lessened as the years went by. He and other members of their family also fell out with Diana "on many occasions," he readily acknowledges.
Her 'favourite spot'
But the level of detail surges again when Spencer comes to the days shortly after her death, particularly around her burial at Althorp, the Spencer family estate.

It is a moment Spencer signals early in the book with his accounting of how the Round Oval, an ornamental lake, was Diana's "favourite spot" in Althorp's parkland, and how a temple in the classical style stands at the far end of the Oval.
"Nobody ever seemed to disturb this spot, and it was where we two youngest children of the family felt safe from the world," he writes. "It was our happy spot."
Sadness, however, is also a big part of the story, and perhaps inevitably, Diana's death becomes a backdrop to the book. It is structured around the emotional eulogy Spencer gave at Diana's funeral.

Each chapter begins with phrases from that fiery speech he famously delivered in front of those gathered in Westminster Abbey on Sept. 6, 1997, where he vowed that William and Harry's "blood family" would protect them and continue Diana's "imaginative and loving" legacy in raising them.
"As with my eulogy, I want to speak on Diana's behalf," Spencer writes early on in Swan Song.

But the structure of the book is in ways chaotic, bouncing around in time and place, which ultimately makes it harder to navigate and take in the overall impression Spencer hopes to create around his sister.
Detours along the way

If Spencer's hope through Swan Song was, as he says, to "give [Diana] hope and applause," it also comes with many detours, including into his own life, and his longstanding antipathy, contempt and grievances over actions of some in the media — notably the paparazzi's relentless pursuit of Diana.
That, of course, is a matter of some considerable criticism and outrage — particularly from her sons — over the years, but doesn't really offer that appreciation Spencer touted as his purpose.

Spencer tells the reader he's writing this book now because with the 30th anniversary of her death approaching, he's been declining "endless, repeated requests to appear in documentaries about her," including from her biographer Andrew Morton and an unnamed nephew, which has prompted speculation it might be Harry. (Some have suggested Spencer's motivations may also be financial, something he has denied.)

Any documentaries that do emerge next year would only be the latest in a long line of explorations of Diana's life, which have been offered with varying degrees of fact and fiction on screen, stage and in the pages of other books.

items: Why did Diana do what she did? Actor Emma Corrin looks for answers as she takes on iconic role in The Crown
Contradictions, charisma and a well-known story: Why it's so hard to become Diana on screen

blocks.text: Swan Song may indeed prove to be Spencer's last public words on his sister, but with that milestone anniversary of her death next year, there is no sense others will stop offering their own narratives of Diana any time soon.

articles.title: More women are taking testosterone to treat menopause symptoms. Does science support that?
articles.summary: Testosterone is touted as a cure-all for menopause symptoms on social media, and more women are now taking it off-label. Scientists want more research.

image.caption: Testosterone's popularity is booming among women. But does science actually back up its use for menopause? Not yet, and certainly not for every single woman, multiple menopause researchers told CBC News. (Carolyn Kaster/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: This is an excerpt from Second Opinion, a weekly analysis of health and medical science news emailed to subscribers Saturday mornings. If you haven't subscribed yet, you can do that by clicking here.
Scroll through social media as a woman of a certain age and you might spot a trend.
Testosterone is being touted as a cure-all for menopause symptoms — everything from a sluggish sex drive to night sweats — by a range of influencers and physicians.
While the hormone isn't approved to treat menopause symptoms in Canada or the U.S., more women are using it off-label. And policymakers are taking note.
In mid-September, American regulators started evaluating testosterone therapy for menopausal women and called on drugmakers to do more women-specific research.

"Women deserve to have testosterone options that are formulated and dosed specifically for them," said Dr. Dorothy Fink, deputy director of the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, at a live-streamed workshop on Sept. 17.
But is there solid science to back up the use of testosterone to treat menopause? Not quite yet, and certainly not for every single woman, multiple menopause researchers told CBC News.
The debate over testosterone is happening against a complex backdrop, as menopausal hormone therapy in all its forms is moving mainstream after years of declining use.

"In the past, a lot of the fear around hormone therapy was really not based on evidence," said Dr. Marie Christakis, a gynecologist and researcher at Weston and O'Born Centre for Mature Women's Health at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto.
"And now a lot of the salesmanship of hormone therapy is also not based on evidence."
Years of caution around hormone therapy
Menopause, in the simplest terms, is when a woman's periods end for good.
The transition time before is marked by dramatic changes in hormone levels, leading many women to experience a range of symptoms: hot flashes, insomnia, vaginal dryness, to name a few.
For some women, it's unpleasant. For others, it can be debilitating.

items: Menopause wellness advocate hopes Manitoba clinic has full spectrum of 'life transition' supports
Does hitting menopause before 40 cause major health issues later in life? Scientists are aiming to find out

blocks.text: Traditional hormone therapy is meant to combat those health impacts, including estrogen-only menopause therapy and combined estrogen and progesterone, which both come in multiple forms: pills, vaginal creams and skin patches.
But there's no one-size-fits-all approach to hormone therapy.

The 2002 publication of a major U.S. clinical trial on conventional menopause treatments was a flashpoint, as it appeared to show that any benefits from combined estrogen-progesterone hormone therapy didn't outweigh higher risks it carried of breast cancer, heart disease and stroke.

Further research uncovered methodological flaws in the initial study, which focused on older, post-menopausal women, skewing their overall risk of cancer and heart issues. Yet the fears around hormone therapy persisted, and use dropped as a result.

items: Experiencing menopause symptoms? Here's what experts say can help
Menopause is a 'freight train' of symptoms, and this B.C. conference aims to help people navigate it

blocks.text: But the tides have turned.

In 2021, the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology issued a guideline indicating that menopausal hormone therapy is the "most effective option" for women to manage symptoms like hot flashes, noting it can be safely used for most women under 60 or who are less than 10 years post-menopause.

Just last year, U.S. officials removed longstanding "black box" warnings about potential risks of cardiovascular disease, stroke, breast cancer and dementia linked to menopause hormone therapies — a move backed by the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada.
There are now more approved, accessible options to manage the transition into menopause.
But the question many women are now facing is, should testosterone be one of them?
Testosterone not part of 'true regime' for menopause care
Testosterone — a sex hormone — is produced at lower levels in women than in men, and gradually declines with age, typically long before the point of menopause.

"The evidence is actually that testosterone levels in pre-menopausal women decrease sometime in the early to mid-thirties," said clinician-scientist Dr. Jerrilyn Prior, a professor emerita of endocrinology and medicine at the University of British Columbia.

items: Why does everyone want to sell me something for my vagina right now?
Does creatine work for menopausal symptoms? Doctors weigh in

blocks.text: There's actually no physiological reason for menopausal women to take testosterone in general, she said, since unlike the sharp drops in the production of estrogen and progesterone, a woman's ovaries continue producing steadily-lower levels of testosterone for years.
"The only situation in which testosterone I think is necessary, and very helpful, is someone who's had their ovaries removed," Prior said.
"They don't have that natural testosterone production anymore."
Vancouver menopause clinic seeks to help those with severe symptoms

The hormone has never really been part of the "true regime" of therapy options for menopause-related symptoms, said Dr. Shafeena Premji, founder and medical director of the Milestone Menopause Centre of Southern Alberta and a board member of the Canadian Menopause Society.
Most research on testosterone and menopause is primarily focused on post-menopausal women who have hypoactive sexual desire disorder, she said.

"This is where a woman has low desire that is causing personal distress," Premji said, explaining how a major drop in libido can be linked to a range of health issues beyond hormones, from other medical conditions to medication side effects and mood disorders.

items: Ottawa announces $5.4M for 5 sexual and reproductive health organizations
Estrogen patch shortage leaves some Albertans in a lurch, looking for alternatives

blocks.text: Body image concerns and life stressors can also play a role, she said, which means treating the condition often requires a thoughtful approach beyond just hormone therapy.
The challenge is that modern women are now bombarded with "misinformation and misguidance" about how to manage menopause, Premji said.
"We can't make false claims and promise things to women when we don't actually have the research to back that up."
New menopause clinic will address gaps in care: Winnipeg doctor
Concern over risks, lack of safety data in women

Amid their ongoing assessment of testosterone's benefits and risks for women, American regulators are requesting public feedback into mid-October, though the evaluation process could last far longer than that.

But as it stands, there's insufficient data to recommend testosterone for broader issues linked to mood, cognition or general well-being, said Rajita Patil, director of the UCLA Comprehensive Menopause Care Program, at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's September workshop held.

She spoke about how oral testosterone is also not recommended because of unfavourable effects on cholesterol levels. Multiple experts also stressed there's concern about broader risks, a lack of long-term safety data in women and the potential for unwanted physical side effects.

"With testosterone, there's a very fine line between [potential benefits and] starting to get hair where you don't want it, and oily skin, and having to wash your hair every two days or something," Prior told CBC News.

items: Gaps in menopause care push some Canadians to pay out of pocket
How Canadian women are finally shedding the shame around menopause

blocks.text: Not every symptom linked to menopause

Women living with menopause should consider getting a full health assessment from a medical professional, Premji said, since aging bodies experience a range of health impacts beyond just changing hormones.
"Not every symptom is always related to perimenopause," she said, referring to the years-long transition phase before menopause hits.
"We have to be able to screen for other medical conditions that could be contributing to symptoms before we attribute everything to menopause."
Despite the buzz and promises of testosterone therapy, Prior also stressed that menopause itself isn't a disease or something that has to be fixed.
She said anyone selling an understudied treatment might just have "something to gain."

articles.title: Mothers crossing the Mexico-U.S. border risk everything to reunite with their children
articles.summary: While the migrant caravans may have disappeared from Tijuana, and this Mexican border city is no longer the waiting room for entry into the U.S., there are still those seeking to cross. Many who risk…

image.caption: Dina Ramos, seen at the Madre Asunta shelter in Tijuana, Mexico, on Sept. 16, was caught days earlier trying to cross the Mexican border to get back to her six children who were all born in the U.S. (Alessandro Molatore/CBC)

blocks.text: Maria says the smugglers formed a human ladder and told her to climb up by grabbing their shoulders and the steel bars of the border wall between Mexico and California.

The human smugglers picked a spot along the border wall near Tecate, a municipality about 50 kilometres east of Tijuana. It was June, and Maria was trying to return to the U.S. to be reunited with her twin sons and husband in California. She was with a group of about five others also trying to cross.
Maria says a young man was the first to scale up the human ladder and over the border wall. She was told to go up next and started to climb.

"Then I heard and saw that [U.S. Border Patrol] trucks started to arrive," said Maria, in an interview earlier this month with CBC News at the Instituto Madre Asunta shelter for women and children in Tijuana.
Mexican moms willing to risk it all to see their kids in the U.S.
Maria says she fell back on the Mexican side and landed among shrubs with thorns and the group started running. She says she doesn't know what happened to the young man who made it over the wall.
CBC News is not using Maria’s full name because she fears repercussions for her attempts to enter the U.S. twice in the past 10 months.
While migrant caravans from Tijuana have disappeared and this Mexican border city of about 2.3 million is no longer the waiting room for entry into the U.S., there are still people seeking to cross.

Many who risk the journey have been separated from their families by deportation, including mothers who are trying to get back to their children, advocates say. And they're choosing more dangerous, clandestine routes that cost tens of thousands of dollars with narrow margins of success.
She says she fell back on the Mexican side and landed among shrubs with thorns and the group started running. She doesn’t know what happened to the young man who had made it over the wall.
Maria says her husband, who is still in California, arranged for her failed attempt to cross the border in June, but she doesn't know how much he paid. "The only thing I know is that we owe money."

items: Mexican woman fighting deportation in Montreal fears for autistic son
Canada’s Mexico visa requirements limit country’s tourism potential, says tour operator

blocks.text: Vitalina Pietrobiassi, the director of the shelter run by the Catholic order of Scalabrinian Missionaries, says the Mexico-U.S. border is a place of "pain" and "separation" for many.
"The women who are deported come here to find a way out of their desperation," said Pietrobiassi.
Smugglers charge up to $25,000 US

Next door, Raul Ochoa is the executive director at House of the Migrant, a shelter for men also run by the Scalabrinians. He says that based on conversations he's had, human smugglers in the area are now charging between $15,000 to $25,000 US to move people across the border.

The low end of the smuggling price spectrum may mean following a guide to a remote spot where surveillance is weak, Ochoa says, adding that paying top dollar could get you guaranteed passage through a port of entry under an arrangement with a U.S. Customs and Border Protection agent.
Crossing into the U.S. right now has a low probability of success, he says, even if one has the money to pay human smugglers known as coyotes.
"The border is basically sealed, there is a lot of security, and the price to pay a coyote is extremely high."

Dina Ramos is also staying at the Instituto Madre Asunta. Ramos, a mother of six children who were all born in the U.S. where she lived undocumented for more than 20 years, says she was caught by U.S. authorities on Sept. 13, while trying to slip across the border.
Ramos would not share details of her crossing attempt, but says she was trying to get back to her family in the U.S. after she returned to Mexico in July to see her ailing parents.
"My children are over there, on the other side, and that's what hurts," she said.

items: Migrants and advocates call on Ottawa for permanent status, with 11 rallies across the country

blocks.text: Ramos says she's desperate to be with her children and plans to find another way across the border.
"One does many things for love," she said.
"I am going to ask for direction from God. I have faith in Him and He is the only one that can help me."
Applying to come to Canada

Ramos was one of more than 10,000 people intercepted since last October by U.S. border authorities in the San Diego Sector. The sector covers roughly 96 km of land border from the Pacific Ocean west of Tijuana to the Tecate region.
This figure is a sharp drop from the approximately 320,000 apprehensions recorded in that area between October 2023 and September 2024, according to U.S. border data.

U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection issued a statement on Sept. 16 saying that apprehensions along the U.S.-Mexico border had dropped by more than 90 per cent since December 2023.

Tijuana immigration lawyer Soraya Vazquez, deputy director of Al Otro Lado, an organization that provides legal and humanitarian support to migrants and refugees, says many of the people still willing to risk crossing the border are deportees trying to get back to their families.
"It's something that is still happening, most of all, yes, with deported mothers who left their families, their children," said Vazquez. "They will always have a yearning to return."
For Maria, staying in Tijuana is not an option. She says she wants to get back to her twin sons — one is set to join the U.S. Marines — and her husband.

Maria, originally from the state of Mexico, has lived undocumented in the U.S. for years. She says she has managed to cross irregularly between the two countries twice. In December 2024 she received word that her oldest son had suffered a massive heart attack at age 29, and she rushed back to Mexico. He died before she arrived and she stayed for a year after.

items: U.S. deporting thousands of Mexican migrants to Central American countries

blocks.text: She says the family considered moving to Canada because her U.S.-born twins would have no issues entering the country.

Maria hired an immigration lawyer in Mexico City who she says got her an appointment with the Canadian embassy in the fall of 2025. At that appointment, she says, a Canadian official took her photo, fingerprints and interviewed her.
"The person who interviewed me told me, 'Good luck,' and that he believed I was a good person," Maria said.

But she says Canadian officials rejected her application and she was never told why. So, in December 2025, she decided to put her life in the hands of human smugglers and cross into the U.S. through the Mexican border state of Sonora, which borders Arizona.
'The dream ends here'

Maria says she was with a group of about half a dozen people who walked for three days through the desert and mountainous borderlands. On the third day, at about 2 or 3 a.m., they believed they had successfully managed to make it across.
"And then all these flashlights turned on," she said.
"It was immigration and they told us, 'Stop walking, don't advance, stand there.' They had dogs."
On the ground at the border wall between the U.S. and Mexico

Maria says she'd been travelling with another mother and her 14-year-old son. She says the mother told her she was trying to save the boy who no longer wanted to go school and was getting involved with people linked to crime.
"She cried. All that effort, all those bruises, all those falls, it stays here, the dream ends here," said Maria.

They were all handcuffed and made to walk what Maria says felt like a long distance to a bus that took them to the Central Arizona Florence Correctional Center about 100 km southeast of Phoenix, Ariz.

items: In the Arizona desert, a race to help migrants who have just crossed the border

blocks.text: Maria was assigned a lawyer who recommended she plead guilty at her court hearing before a judge in Tucson, Ariz. After her plea, Maria was deported back to Mexico about a week before Christmas. She'd spent about two weeks incarcerated.
Despite her two failed attempts, Maria says she plans to try again to get to her sons.
"It's tough. At first, it's a nightmare, but that nightmare can turn into a dream," she said.
"A dream I want to reach in the future … to be with my family, to be united."

articles.title: As Cineplex considers a potential sale, audiences appear to be rediscovering movie theatre magic
articles.summary: As Cineplex indicates a sale might be in its future, experts and the company's own financial reports suggest movie theatres are seeing a resurgence in popularity in Canada — thanks in part to younger…

image.caption: In a news release this week, Cineplex said it is undergoing a strategic review, and that selling the company may be part of its future. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

As Cineplex indicates a sale might be in its future, experts and the company's own financial reports suggest movie theatres are seeing a resurgence in popularity in Canada — thanks in part to younger generations of cinephiles.
Financial reports show company saw year-over-year increase in attendance in first half of the year

As Cineplex indicates a sale might be in its future, experts and the company's own financial reports suggest movie theatres are seeing a resurgence in popularity in Canada, thanks in part to younger generations of cinephiles.

A memo released this week announcing Bill Walker as the company's new CEO said Cineplex has initiated a strategic review to look at opportunities "to enhance and maximize value for all shareholders" that could include selling the company.

"While we remain highly confident in the company’s future prospects, we are committed to evaluating all available opportunities and remain open-minded regarding potential outcomes," said Phyllis Yaffe, head of Cineplex's board, in the memo.

The news comes after Cineplex reported box office revenues of close to $98 million in August, its highest monthly box office performance in the company's history, driven by the release of summer blockbusters The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
The company also reported it saw a 12.7 per cent increase in theatre attendance in the first half of 2026 compared to the same time period last year, with a 12.3 per cent increase in revenues.

items: Cineplex may be going up for sale, company says in announcement of new CEO
Cineplex is launching 'surprise' movie premieres, but will it help bring audiences back to theatres?

blocks.text: Still, movie theatre attendance hasn't fully returned to pre-pandemic levels, with a recent Telefilm Canada study finding ticket consumption per capita in 2024 was about half of what it was in 2019.
However, the report also noted that 2019 was a year that saw the release of several blockbuster films, and that 2024 ticket consumption was only four per cent lower than 2014.

While moviegoing may not be what it once was, it's still an important part of popular culture, said Paul Moore, a professor at Toronto Metropolitan University who studies the history of moviegoing and movie theatres.
"I don't think a change in ownership is going to change the place that Cineplex has in the retail landscape or in our cultural landscape," he said.
"There's no hint that megaplexes are losing so much money that somebody actually wants to shut them down and rework their real estate."
Want to watch The Odyssey the way Christopher Nolan shot it? You might have to wait weeks
Young people filling seats

The same Telefilm report also suggests that young people aren't replacing going to the cinema with streaming, at least not entirely. The report found that 85 per cent of respondents under 35 said they were moviegoers, compared to 54 per cent of those 35 and up.
That's been the case throughout most of history, Moore said, since movies have always catered to young people.
"So it's good to see that continuity with the past," he said.

items: Young people grew up in the digital age. So why do they love movies on film?
YouTube already had a place in Hollywood. The success of Backrooms and Obsession proves it's undeniable

blocks.text: Independent cinemas are also seeing a bump in attendance year-over-year, said Sonya Yokota William, the director of the Network of Independent Canadian Exhibitors.
William attributes the bump in part to younger, Gen-Z audiences that are "more curious and more adventurous and happy to go out and see something that maybe they wouldn't have before."
But with Cineplex taking in close to 74 per cent of all box-office revenue in Canada, William said she worries that any changes in ownership could "really hurt cinema going in this country."

However, Moore pointed out that the majority of Canada's cinemas were under foreign ownership for most of their history, back when Famous Players — a subsidiary of U.S-based Paramount — dominated the country's movie theatre industry.

Moore said he doesn't think much has changed since Famous Players was bought by Cineplex in 2005 in terms of what's offered to moviegoers. He also pointed out that Landmark Cinemas, its nearest competitor in Canada, is owned by a Belgium company that offers similar content.
"In general, the fact that Cineplex is owned by a Canadian company is really making very little difference to the kinds of movies that it's showing and its role in the Canadian film industry."

items: The magic of going to the theatre isn’t about the movie. It’s about watching it with strangers
Toronto cinema says it was forced to cancel screenings over decades-old, unofficial 'zone' system

blocks.text: In any event, the sale of Cineplex to new owners seems to be only a possibility at this point.
In its memo, the company said "no decisions have been made."
"There can be no assurance that the Strategic Review will result in any transaction, agreement or other strategic outcome," the memo read.

The chain was last up for sale in 2019, when the company agreed to a $2.8-billion buyout by U.K.-based Cineworld Group PLC. But the deal fell through duing the COVID-19 pandemic when theatres were forced to abruptly shut down.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sarah Petz is a Toronto-based senior writer with the CBC News live pages team. Born and raised in Manitoba, her career has taken her across three provinces, multiple cities and to northern Uganda.

articles.title: Some TV meteorologists want to talk about climate change. Not everyone wants to hear it
articles.summary: Broadcast meteorologists usually talk about the weather, but as the planet warms, many weather presenters feel they must talk about climate change. It can be a tough balancing act — and it can have…

image.caption: John. Morales presenting a weather broadcast on Hurricane Melissa on Oct. 28, 2025. Morales said he was inspired to start talking about climate change in his work after a 1997 meeting of meteorologists at the White House. (Submitted by John Morales)

blocks.text: LISTEN | The weatherman who spoke the truth — and paid the price:
What on Earth?25:06The weatherman who spoke the truth – and paid the price
John Morales remembers the moment he broke down on air.

The veteran meteorologist, who works for the WTVJ television station in Miami, had been talking about climate change in his weather reports for decades. But in October 2024, after watching Hurricane Milton rapidly gain strength off the coasts of Florida and Mexico, he began tearing up.

"I was delivering the facts, but suddenly I realized how strong of a hurricane that could be, how many victims it could take, how many lives it could ruin," he told What on Earth? host Johanna Wagstaffe at the Climate Week NYC conference.

"These events are happening with such frequency now, and there’s so many people in harm’s way, that I feel more compelled to call for action, to have people prepare for the worst, because the worst is happening, more and more often."

Hurricane Milton would go on to kill 15 people across the U.S. and Mexico, according to a National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) report. NOAA estimated Milton caused a further 27 indirect deaths related to preparation, clean-up and power failures, not to mention $34.3 billion US in damages in Florida.

items: Southwestern Mexico braces for arrival of 'extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo
El Niño moves into record-breaking territory

blocks.text: Morales said his reaction was a mix of climate anxiety, anticipatory grief for the victims and frustration.
"For 20 or 25 years, I’ve been communicating on climate, providing climate context to audiences, empowering them through education, to demand action on climate," he said.
"Yet hardly anything has been done."
It wasn’t always like this. Growing up in Puerto Rico, Morales was excited by the storms he now often dreads. The fascination led him to a career as a meteorologist.

At a meeting of meteorologists at the White House in 1997, vice-president Al Gore said something that inspired Morales. Gore asked why meteorologists comment on events like shooting stars, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions but not climate change. Morales said it was the catalyst for talking about climate change on air.
"At first it was difficult, and then I started to see more opportunities and less resistance from managers in newsrooms for me to do that," he said.
"My hand was getting slapped less and less."
El Niño-fuelled heat could kill half a million people by February: study
Today, Morales says, he rarely gets pushback from audiences, and Miamians often thank him for his climate coverage.

And he’s got a lot of company now, as just one of many meteorologists who incorporate climate change into their work in front of the green screen. Morales lauds the work of his peer Elisa Raffa, who takes this approach in more conservative cities across the Midwest, explaining the phenomenon in a way that resonates with those audiences.
But for some broadcast meteorologists, it can be a dangerous undertaking.
The cost of communicating climate

In 2019, Chris Gloninger was working as a meteorologist for NBC’s WBTS television station in Boston, one of the biggest markets in the country, when he successfully pitched the station on a weekly climate change segment.
In 2021, he decided he needed to talk about climate change in a more skeptical, conservative market. He took a job with KCCI in Des Moines, Iowa.
"I saw there was an opportunity to talk climate in a part of the country where it wasn’t being talked about," he told Joanna Wagstaffe at Climate Week NYC.
"That was a difficult decision, and honestly it was leaving a dream job, but I was up for the challenge, because I thought it was that important of an issue."

It meant trading his dedicated climate change segment for 10- to 15-second tidbits on climate trends and renewable energy during weathercasts. Still, Gloninger knew that global warming had powerful implications for Iowa’s large agricultural sector, and he was undeterred by the hate mail. He took the approach of talking about the financial costs of climate change and energy independence to get through to Iowans.
"I had to make sure that I was not an activist. I had to make sure that I was not trying to be an educator," he said.
"I just simply wanted to be the local meteorologist that was showing trends, and explaining ... why things were happening the way they were happening."
This year's hurricane season has been eerily quiet — here's why

But everything changed with one email. In 2022, a viewer sent Gloninger a death threat referencing the attempted assassination of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanagh just weeks earlier. A man with a gun, a knife and zip ties had been arrested outside Kavanagh’s home.
In August 2022, police in Iowa charged Danny Hancock, 63, who pleaded guilty to third-degree harassment and received a fine, the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported.
After that, Gloninger said he felt a lack of support from the station. He says KCCI began pushing him to stop talking about climate change and science. He left in 2023.
"They did a 180 on what they agreed with when they hired me," he said. "No viewer email stung as much as the response that I received from them."
KCCI and its parent company, Hearst Television, have not responded to CBC’s request for comment.
Gloninger now works for an environmental engineering company in Cape Cod, Mass. He enjoys his work, but the transition has been hard.
"It felt like I was giving up on the dream that second-grade Chris had," he said of his last day as a broadcast meteorologist. "I miss it. I really do."
Are things different in Canada?

Chris Scott, chief meteorologist at Pelmorex — The Weather Network’s parent company — said he doesn’t think climate change is a controversial topic in Canada. But he also believes viewers aren’t really tuning in for it.

"When people come to The Weather Network on a daily basis, they are looking for information to help them make decisions, like how to dress, 'what is my drive going to be like? When can I do an outdoor activity?'" he said.
Scott said the network’s approach is to incorporate climate change to reporting on extreme weather events, such as the wildfires that ravaged parts of the country this summer.

Jason Thistlethwaite, an associate professor at the University of Waterloo’s Faculty of Environment, was co-author on a 2019 study that interviewed Canadian weather broadcasters, including the CBC, on their role in communicating climate change. The broadcasters reported a range of barriers, from fears of poor audience and station management reception to a lack of time and newsroom resources to do segments.

"I wouldn’t go so far as to say that for every six o’clock news broadcast, that a meteorologist needs to be spending a few seconds saying, 'Well, today is quite clearly being influenced by global climate change,'" Thistlethwaite said in an interview.

items: It's almost the end of September. Where are all the hurricanes?
Northeast B.C. faces warmer future and more extreme weather threats, researchers say

blocks.text: "Where I think there is opportunity is sort of to give them opportunities to do their own stories."
For Gloninger, climate change is an essential part of the job.
"As meteorologists, we get into this to save and protect life and property," he said. "If you’re not doing that, you’re failing your audience."

articles.title: Lula bans fixed-odds sports betting a week before Brazilian elections
articles.summary:
President’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggest

Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning…

blocks.text: Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning fixed-odds sports betting just over a week before the first round of the presidential election, in a move he said was designed to tackle the pervasive problem of families falling into debt.
The decision ends the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of betting.

The provisional executive order comes into force immediately but will need congressional approval within 120 days to remain in effect. It prohibits new deposits into accounts and gives users of betting platforms until 5 October to withdraw their funds.

Lula’s government has also drafted a bill to establish criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting – the most common and dominant type of online sports betting – such as promoting them and using personal data to solicit punters.
“I made the decision to take a hard, drastic and necessary measure,” he told journalists in São Paulo. “It’s like cancer, you take out the tumour, or the tumour will kill us.”
Lula had also criticised the betting industry earlier this week at the United Nations general assembly, accusing it of “transforming addiction into profit” and of “destroying homes”.
Polls suggest a ban enjoys widespread support among Brazilians. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s main rival in the upcoming election, accused the current leader of an “electoral measure”.

Brazil’s president has sharply criticised online betting at least since April, when he called for a ban. The public backlash against it grew during the Fifa World Cup when advertisements were ubiquitous and the number of people betting surged.

Betting and gambling are estimated to cost Brazilian society 38.8bn reais (£5.6bn) annually and increases suicide and depression, according to a 2025 study by the nonprofit Institute of Studies for Health Policies.

The country’s central bank estimated last year that Brazilians spend about 30bn reais on bets each month. That figure included spending by beneficiaries of the cash-transfer federal welfare programme Bolsa Familia (family grant), which was blocked from those platforms last year.
Lawmakers, including many from Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal party, struck down a Lula order for tax hikes on online betting and virtual casinos in October last year.

Gambling is illegal in Brazil, but the country opened the gates to online betting in 2018 during the presidency of Michel Temer. The phenomenon snowballed under the watch of the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro’s father.

In December 2023, Lula signed a law to regulate and tax betting companies for the first time. Months later, his administration blocked more than 2,000 online betting websites that were designated as irregular, including some linked to criminal organisations such as the First Capital Command from São Paulo and the Red Command of Rio de Janeiro. It was part of a national push to regulate the sector.

Lula and members of his administration have spoken about banning online betting as necessary to both close a drain to the country’s economy and to tackle a public health issue, as many Brazilians are addicted and in financial difficulties due to spending their money on these platforms.
Business analysts say that revenues for sports betting, one of the betting models banned on Friday, are estimated at more than $4bn (£3bn) per year in Brazil, one of the biggest markets in the world.
Before Friday’s move, Brazil’s main football clubs sounded the alarm after betting companies reportedly warned that their sponsorships would end immediately if the government banned betting.
They said the move could lead to the end of Brazilian football, a claim mocked by some social media users in the football-mad country.

articles.title: TikTok reaches first state settlement in US over teen safety claims, agrees to user limits
articles.summary: Alabama secures $100 million settlement with TikTok, mandating new usage limits and age-verification measures to protect teens, as the state claims the platform endangers youth and misleads consumers…

blocks.text: Alabama said on Friday it had reached a settlement with TikTok and its Chinese parent company, ByteDance, that requires the social media platform to impose new usage limits and enhanced age-verification measures for users in the state, resolving claims that the platform endangered children and misled consumers about its safety.

The agreement, which came days before a scheduled trial, calls for TikTok to implement changes for teenagers in Alabama including a two-hour daily time limit, pauses after 15 minutes of use and stricter age checks.

TikTok will pay Alabama at least $100 million under the settlement, but the state’s payout could grow to $300 million if 40 other attorneys general sign on to similar agreements with the company within a specified timeframe, according to the settlement.
“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” a spokesperson for TikTok’s US operations said in a statement.

The deal marks TikTok’s first settlement with a state in the sweeping litigation over social media’s impact on teen well-being. Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall sued the company last year, and at least 27 other states and Washington, D.C., have brought similar lawsuits.
“This is a great day for Alabama parents,” Marshall said in announcing the agreement.

The trial, which had been scheduled to kick off Monday in Montgomery state court and expected to last two to three weeks, had been expected to provide a rare look inside TikTok, which has settled prior cases selected for trial and sought to keep details of its operations from public view.

Alabama had claimed TikTok’s endless stream of videos makes it the most addictive social media platform and that its algorithm pushes young users toward increasingly intense content about violence and self-harm, contributing to a teen mental health crisis and causing the number of emergency room visits for self-harm in the state to “skyrocket.”

The lawsuit accused TikTok of falsely claiming it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users in order to have its app rated safe for teens in app stores run by Google, Apple and Microsoft and of misleading users about the Chinese government’s access to US users’ data.

TikTok has said it designed its platform with teen safety as a key priority and argued that Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act shields online platforms from liability over user-generated content.

In addition to the states’ cases, TikTok faces thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts and municipalities over its alleged impact on young users’ mental health. Meta Platforms, Snap Inc and Alphabet’s YouTube are also defendants in many of these cases.
With the settlement in Alabama, TikTok has settled all cases selected for trial against it, including claims by five young people and a Kentucky school district.

Alabama’s lawsuit claimed TikTok asks users to self-report their ages, but it also allows users to evade its questions about their age by viewing videos without creating an account, which still allows the company to collect data on their viewing habits. The lack of an effective age restriction makes things like “Kids Mode,” which curates content for young users, entirely useless, according to the lawsuit.

The state also claimed the platform traps kids in so-called “filter bubbles,” feeding them increasingly intense content on subjects that capture their attention, including violent or harmful material.

Last month, ​Meta reached a sweeping $17.1 billion settlement with 47 states, Washington, D.C., and US territories. Meta, which ​did not admit wrongdoing, agreed to make changes to teens’ access to Instagram and Facebook as part of the deal and conditioned $5 billion of the payout on TikTok, Snap ​and YouTube’s adoption of those terms. TikTok has not said anything publicly about the deal.
Like the Meta settlement, Alabama’s deal with TikTok would require the company to adopt additional restrictions if its rivals Snap, Google and Meta make similar changes.
Those measures could further limit teens’ time on social media apps and restrict overnight access, according to the filing.
Although the settlement applies only in Alabama, major platform changes could prove difficult to implement on a state-by-state basis. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: India and Pakistan traded accusations at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Friday, with Islamabad criticizing India's stance on Kashmir and New Delhi accusing Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism.
Addressing the General Assembly, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for "a just and fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute," alleging human rights violations in the region.
Sharif also brought up the military clashes last year between the uneasy neighbors, calling them "external aggression from India under a false pretext."

Pakistan considers Indian missile strikes on May 7 to be the start of the low-level conflict, which ran for less than a week, while India contends that the strikes were retaliation for an attack in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in April last year.
He added that India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance had no legal basis and accused New Delhi of "weaponizing" water.

India rejected Sharif's remarks. First Secretary at India's UN mission Petal Gahlot accused Pakistan of "terrorism, deceit and duplicity" and said Islamabad's support for cross-border terrorism would have consequences.
Gahlot also criticized Pakistan's military establishment and its treatment of minorities, while reiterating India's position that Jammu and Kashmir is an integral part of the country.

articles.title: Duterte camp flags 62,000-plus evidence ahead of ICC trial, seeks 10,000 cap
articles.summary: The defense team of former President Rodrigo Duterte has asked the International Criminal Court to limit the prosecution’s evidence to 10,000 items, saying the case record has ballooned to more…

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 3:25pm

MANILA, Philippines — The defense team of former President Rodrigo Duterte has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to limit the prosecution’s evidence to 10,000 items, saying the case record has ballooned to more than 62,000 items ahead of his trial.
Defense counsel Peter Haynes filed the motion before ICC Trial Chamber III on Friday, September 25, citing the volume and quality of the evidence disclosed by the prosecution.
The defense said the prosecution initially disclosed 5,275 evidence items during the confirmation phase but later expanded the list to 62,130, a 978% increase.
The prosecution’s current List of Evidence contains 19,238 items, according to the defense.

“The Defence has no ability to read this volume of evidence prior to trial. However, even a cursory review demonstrates that much of the disclosed material is of extremely limited or no relevance to the charges in this case,” Haynes said.
The defense said the disclosure includes more than 320,000 pages of documents and 1,000 audio-visual materials.

“The sheer volume of material, disclosed to the Defence three months before the start of trial, undermines Mr Duterte’s right to adequate time for the preparation of his defence pursuant to Article 67(1)(b),” Haynes said.
The defense estimated that reviewing all the documentary evidence just once would take about 16,000 person-hours.
“On a conservative estimate of three minutes per page, it would take 16,000 person hours to review every disclosed item of documentary evidence just once,” Haynes said.

The defense also flagged problems with the evidence, including incorrect descriptions, dates and metadata, detached pages, illegible or blank items, duplicate documents, and untranslated or untranscribed audio and video files.
They said proceeding with the case under the current disclosure would also affect Duterte’s right to a timely trial.
“Proceeding to trial on this basis would undermine the efficiency of proceedings and, by consequence, Mr Duterte’s right to trial without undue delay,” Haynes said.
Defense asks for 10,000-item case record
Instead of seeking to postpone the trial, the defense proposed that the prosecution sort through the evidence and create a new case record containing a maximum of 10,000 items.
The proposed record would include exculpatory evidence, as well as duly reviewed and triaged Rule 77 and incriminating evidence.
“A reduction from 62,130 to 10,000 is significant,” the defense said.
They said the remaining evidence would still be accessible to Duterte’s lawyers, who would have to “read, watch, listen to, review and tag” the original case record.
Haynes asked the chamber to order the prosecution to work with the ICC Registry to create the new case record by October 7.
The defense said this would allow the trial to proceed as scheduled on November 30.
Duterte’s defense team is due to file its pre-trial brief on October 30.
Duterte remains detained
Duterte remains detained at the ICC in The Hague, where he faces crimes against humanity charges over killings linked to his war on drugs.
The 81-year-old former president appeared in person before the ICC on September 16 during the third status conference.
Trial Chamber III later ruled that he should remain detained, citing the likelihood that he could abscond or obstruct or endanger the investigation or court proceedings.
His trial is scheduled to begin on Nov. 30, 2026. — with a report from Cristina Chi
